items.prompt: State what is meant by the term tourism.
items.canonical_answer: Travel away from a person's usual home for leisure, business, sport or visiting friends and family, normally involving at least one night away, which brings spending to the receiving area.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - travel away from home for leisure or business, normally with at least one night away. A definition that names what the term covers earns the mark; a day trip to work does not.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the growth of tourism in relation to the main attractions of the physical and human landscape

items.prompt: Explain why international tourism grew so rapidly between 1950 and 2019.
items.canonical_answer: Jet aircraft and later budget airlines cut the cost and time of travel, so long journeys became affordable. Incomes rose in many countries, so households had money to spare on holidays. Paid holidays spread through the world of work, which gave people the time as well as the money. Package tours and then internet booking made arranging a trip easy, so people who had never travelled began to go.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: how cheaper air travel cut the cost and time; because incomes rose there was spare money; so paid holidays gave the time; which easier booking then added. Accept any three causes, each linked to the effect it had on travel.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the growth of tourism in relation to the main attractions of the physical and human landscape

items.prompt:
The table shows approximate world international tourist arrivals:

| year | arrivals / millions |
|---|---|
| 1950 | 25 |
| 1970 | 170 |
| 1990 | 440 |
| 2010 | 950 |
| 2019 | 1400 |

Describe the trend shown.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows arrivals rising continuously over the whole period, from 25 million in 1950 to about 1 400 million in 2019. The rise gets steeper: the growth between 1990 and 2019 was 960 million, 1400 - 440 = 960, while the growth between 1950 and 1990 was 415 million, 440 - 25 = 415. So the last three decades of the period brought well over half of the total increase, which means the growth accelerated as travel became cheaper.
marking_guidance: Reading: the trend read from the table - a strong, continuous rise across the whole period (1 mark).

Figures: the values quoted at two points, such as 25 million and 1 400 million, so the size of the change is shown (1 mark); the faster later growth identified with the figures from the table (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the growth of tourism in relation to the main attractions of the physical and human landscape

items.prompt: A coastal town in southern Africa has a sheltered sandy bay, buildings from its time as a colonial port, and a music festival every August. Suggest why the town attracts more than one kind of visitor.
items.canonical_answer: The bay suits visitors who come to swim, sail and sunbathe, because sheltered sand and a warm sea are what such visitors look for. The old port buildings attract sightseers and photographers interested in the town's past. The August festival draws visitors who travel for music and local culture, so the town's physical and human attractions together widen the kinds of visitor it receives.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: each reason uses this example - the bay, the old buildings or the festival - and names which visitors it draws, because an attraction explains the resort only when linked to what the visitor does there.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the growth of tourism in relation to the main attractions of the physical and human landscape

items.prompt: Asked to explain why a resort is popular, a learner writes: "It has a beach, a museum, mountains and a good climate." Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has listed attractions without saying why they attract tourists, so the answer explains nothing: a list names features but never links them to visitors. A developed answer says what each visitor does there - the beach draws swimmers and sunbathers, the museum draws sightseers, the mountains draw hikers - because an attraction attracts only when the visitors it draws are named.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the error named - a bare list, which is a description of features, not a mistake the resort makes but a wrong way to answer.
1 mark: the correct idea instead - each attraction linked to the visitors it draws, for example the beach and swimming.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Describe and explain the growth of tourism in relation to the main attractions of the physical and human landscape

items.prompt: Describe two benefits tourism brings to the people of a receiving area.
items.canonical_answer: Jobs: hotels, restaurants and tour guiding employ local people directly, and farms, craft sellers and transport services supply the industry, so the benefit of the spending spreads beyond the hotels themselves. Foreign income: visitors arrive with money earned elsewhere and spend it locally, which is an opportunity because the area gains income it did not have to create at home.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per benefit, to 2: each advantage named and developed with because or so - jobs, or income entering the area. An opportunity taken to its consequence earns the mark; a bare list of benefits does not.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Evaluate the benefits and disadvantages of tourism to receiving areas

items.prompt: Describe two problems tourism can cause for the people who live in a receiving area.
items.canonical_answer: Seasonal, low-paid work: many hotel and tour jobs last only for the busy months, which means workers face weeks without wages each year. Rising prices: demand from visitors can push up the cost of land, food and services, so residents on local incomes are priced out of their own town in the busy season.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per problem, to 2: each disadvantage developed with because or so - seasonality and pay, or prices and crowding. A limitation stated without its consequence for local people does not earn the mark.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Evaluate the benefits and disadvantages of tourism to receiving areas

items.prompt: A town's shops report that visitor spending has doubled in five years. A survey of residents the same year found that most of them find the town unaffordable in the busy season. Suggest how far the town council is right to call tourism a success for the town.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement is only partly right. The evidence for success is real: visitor spending has doubled in five years, which means more turnover for shops and more jobs in serving the visitors. But the survey shows the costs are unevenly shared: residents on local wages face unaffordable prices in the very season the money arrives, so the people who host the tourism do not all share the benefit. The better judgement is that tourism has succeeded for the town's businesses but not yet for its residents, since the figures show gains and losses going to different groups.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a stated decision on how far the council's claim holds (1 mark).
Because: both sides weighed against the evidence given - doubled spending set against the affordability survey (1 mark).
So the judgement is refined rather than accepted flat, using the data in the stem - the decision names who gains and who loses (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Evaluate the benefits and disadvantages of tourism to receiving areas

items.prompt: Asked to describe the effects of tourism on local people, a learner writes about litter on the beach and footpath erosion. Explain the error.
items.canonical_answer: The learner has written about the natural environment when the question asks about local people, and the two are not the same group. Impacts are sorted by who or what feels them: local people feel jobs, wages, prices and crowding, while the environment feels litter and erosion. In fact an answer about people should name employment, prices or services; instead this answer has described a different question from the one asked.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the confusion named - environment impacts written instead of impacts on local people, which is not the same thing.
1 mark: the correct idea - impacts sorted by who or what feels them, with a people example such as jobs, wages or prices.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Evaluate the benefits and disadvantages of tourism to receiving areas

items.prompt: State what is meant by a receiving area.
items.canonical_answer: The place tourists travel to and spend their money in, whose businesses and residents host the visitors.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - the place that receives the tourists and their spending. The term is defined from the visitors' point of view: it is where they go, not where they come from.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Evaluate the benefits and disadvantages of tourism to receiving areas

items.prompt: Describe two features of the jobs tourism creates in a receiving area.
items.canonical_answer: Many of the jobs are seasonal, concentrated in the busy months of the year, and much of the work is low paid, such as cleaning, serving and unskilled guiding. A second feature is that the work is both direct, in hotels and restaurants, and indirect, in the farms, craft workshops and bus services that supply the industry.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, to 2: seasonality, low pay, or the direct and indirect split - each a fact about the employment tourism creates, not a general point about jobs.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Evaluate the benefits and disadvantages of tourism to receiving areas

items.prompt: A gorge trail used by about 50 walkers a day is now cut about 1 metre deep in places, and plants on both sides are trampled bare. Suggest three management actions that would make the trail's use sustainable.
items.canonical_answer: A raised boardwalk or a hardened surface along the eroded line would carry walkers without further trampling, because feet would leave the soil surface. A single marked route with barriers would keep visitors to one line, so the trampled plants on either side could recover. A daily limit on walker numbers, or a fee used to repair the path, would slow the damage; here the resource being managed is the gorge itself, so the attraction survives the visits.
marking_guidance: 1 mark each, to 3: each action must fit this example - the eroded path and the trampled plants - and be linked with because or so to the effect it has on the damage. Boardwalk, marked route, caps or fees all fit the resource given.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Demonstrate an understanding that careful management of tourism is required in order for it to be sustainable

items.prompt: A nature reserve capped its visitor numbers at 500 a day. Income from entry fees has stayed level, and the reserve reports that its eroded ground has begun to recover. Suggest how far the cap is a successful management strategy.
items.canonical_answer: The judgement is that the cap is largely successful. The evidence is that the eroded ground is recovering, so the damage that would have driven visitors away is being reversed, and income has stayed level, which means the limit has not cost the reserve its revenue. Against that, visitors turned away on busy days may go elsewhere, so access carries some cost. On balance the strategy succeeds because it protects what the visitors come to see while keeping the money that pays for the protection - the evidence of both recovery and income supports it.
marking_guidance: Judgement: a stated decision on how successful the cap is (1 mark).
Because: the decision weighed against the evidence - recovering ground and level income set against turned-away visitors (1 mark).
So the answer weighs both sides rather than accepting the strategy flat; credit a judgement backed by the data given (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Demonstrate an understanding that careful management of tourism is required in order for it to be sustainable

items.prompt:
A park introduced a daily visitor cap and a network of marked trails in 2015. The table shows its figures for two years:

| year | visitors per year | eroded trail length / km |
|---|---|---|
| 2012 | 140 000 | 18 |
| 2019 | 95 000 | 7 |

Describe what the table shows about the management.
items.canonical_answer: The table shows visitor numbers falling from 140 000 to 95 000 after the cap, and the eroded trail length falling with them, from 18 km to 7 km. The pattern suggests the management reduced both pressure and damage: fewer visitors and the marked trail network together, so the recovery shows in the figures.
marking_guidance: Reading: the table shows two falling values - visitors and eroded length - read across the two years (1 mark).

Figures: the values quoted for both years, so the size of each fall is shown (1 mark); the link made between the management and the recovery, which means the figures are used to judge the strategy (1 mark).
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Demonstrate an understanding that careful management of tourism is required in order for it to be sustainable

items.prompt: State what is meant by sustainable tourism.
items.canonical_answer: Tourism that meets the needs of visitors, the industry and local people today without reducing the ability of future visitors and residents to meet theirs, by protecting the landscape, wildlife and culture that attract the visitors.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning - present needs met without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs. A definition that names what is protected - environment or culture - shows the term is understood.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: Demonstrate an understanding that careful management of tourism is required in order for it to be sustainable

items.prompt: For Etosha National Park in Namibia, describe two features that attract visitors.
items.canonical_answer: Artificial waterholes beside the rest camps, such as Okaukuejo, where elephants, lions and the park's black rhinos come to drink, giving reliable game viewing. And the great salt pan at the park's centre, with the dry woodland and grassland around it that carry the herds visitors come to watch.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per feature, to 2: each a characteristic of the named park - the waterholes, the lit waterhole at Okaukuejo, the pan, the rest camps or the wildlife. A general point about parks earns nothing.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: A case study of an area where tourism is important

items.prompt: For the area around Etosha National Park, explain why tourism is important to local people.
items.canonical_answer: Conservation fees and rest-camp wages matter in a dry region with few other employers, so families earn money that farming alone does not provide. Because the wildlife stays protected, the earnings continue year after year. Neighbouring communal conservancies receive levies from joint-venture lodges, so tourism income reaches villages outside the park gates as well. This example shows tourism working as a foundation of the regional economy, not just as a bonus.
marking_guidance: 1 mark per developed point, to 4: each reason rests on this example - the fees, the rest camps, the conservancies, the joint-venture lodges - and is linked with because or so to the benefit it brings. Points about the park's scenery alone, without its people, do not answer the question asked.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: A case study of an area where tourism is important

items.prompt: State what is meant by a communal conservancy in Namibia.
items.canonical_answer: A registered area where a local community holds the rights to manage and benefit from the wildlife on its land, earning income from tourism and from regulated hunting.
marking_guidance: 1 mark: the meaning of the term - a community's registered rights to manage and benefit from its wildlife. The definition needs both parts: the community, and the benefit it earns.
items.provenance: Authored for the 0460 learner resource from the topic 3.4 claim ledger.
objective_titles: A case study of an area where tourism is important

items.prompt: For a named area where tourism is important, describe what attracts visitors and explain how tourism benefits local people there and is managed so that it stays sustainable. [7]
items.canonical_answer:
Etosha National Park in northern Namibia, about 22 000 square kilometres of dry woodland and grassland around a vast salt pan, attracts visitors with reliable wildlife viewing: artificial waterholes at the Okaukuejo, Halali and Namutoni rest camps draw elephants, lions and the black rhinos the park is known for protecting, and Okaukuejo's waterhole is lit at night. Roughly 200 000 visitors a year entered in the late 2010s (rounded figure).

Tourism benefits local people because the region is dry with few other employers: conservation fees and rest-camp wages are a foundation of the local economy, and neighbouring communal conservancies receive levies from joint-venture lodges, so the income reaches villages outside the gates. The park is managed so the visits can continue: beds are capped at the three state rest camps, day visitors pay a conservation fee, and speed limits and a ban on off-road driving protect the pan and its animals. The fees fund anti-poaching work, so the wildlife that draws the visitors is protected by the visits themselves.
marking_guidance: Level 1 (1-3): simple statements about attractions or jobs, with no named example or only general points about tourism.
Level 2 (4-6): developed and linked statements about a named area, capped at 5 if no named example is given.

Level 3 (7): comprehensive statements with place-specific detail - Etosha and its pan, the Okaukuejo, Halali and Namutoni rest camps, the 200 000 visitors, the conservancies and their levies, the bed cap and the conservation fee - covering the attractions, the benefits and the management.

items.prompt:
The table shows visitor numbers at a beach resort in the southern hemisphere, in thousands per month:

| month | visitors / thousands |
|---|---|
| November | 30 |
| December | 90 |
| January | 110 |
| February | 95 |
| June | 8 |
| July | 10 |

(a) Identify the month with the fewest visitors. [1]
(b) Describe the pattern of visitor numbers the table shows. [2]
(c) Suggest why visitor numbers rise so steeply between November and December. [3]
(d) Suggest two problems the resort's workers face in June and July. [2]
items.canonical_answer:
(a) June, with 8 thousand visitors.
(b) The numbers peak in the southern-hemisphere summer: a steep rise from November to January, when 110 thousand visit, then a fall through February. Winter is quiet, with under 10 thousand in June and July, so the resort has a strong summer season and a near-empty winter.
(c) The school holidays begin in December, so families are free to travel; the Christmas break brings visitors to the coast; and the summer sea and weather suit swimming, which draws holiday-makers to a beach resort in its hottest weeks.
(d) Seasonal unemployment: many hotel and restaurant jobs end after the summer, so workers lose their wages for the winter months. And hours are cut in the few places that stay open, which means lower pay even for workers still employed.
marking_guidance: Resource: parts (a) and (b) are read from the table - 1 mark for the month identified; 2 marks for the pattern described with figures from the resource, the summer peak and the winter trough both named.
Marks: part (c) is worth 3 marks - three reasons suggested, each linked to the resort and its season; school holidays, Christmas or the summer weather all fit.
Figures: part (d) is worth 2 marks - two problems for the workers, developed with evidence such as lost wages or cut hours; answers that use the off-season values earn credit.
